tone_statements.quote: -ga verbe sfx accompli ; mot verbal qui envisage le processus comme effectivement réalisé ou devant sûrement se réaliser ; postposé à verbe, relève le ton final du verbe qui précède Kali mꞌaisin̰ga dɛpɛlɛ. Ton habit, je vais lui faire un ourlet.
tone_statements.translation: -ga verb suffix, completive; verbal word that views the process as actually realised or sure to be realised; postposed to the verb, it raises the final tone of the preceding verb. Kali m'aisin̰ga dɛpɛlɛ. Your garment, I am going to hem it.
tone_statements.summary: Tone inventory not stated; orthography unmarked for tone; one grammatical-tone process noted (completive -ga raises the verb's final tone).

tone_statements.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 1990. Furu et Bagiro : l'extension oubanguienne des langues « sara » [Persée record title: L'extension oubanguienne des langues « sara »]. Journal des Africanistes 60(1): 77-106.
tone_statements.quote: Une étude comparative en cours17, qui porte sur les systèmes tonals de plusieurs d'entre elles, tend à prouver qu'une branche « occidentale », constituée des langues parlées en RCA et au Tchad (carte III), s'est historiquement détachée de l'ensemble primitif : les systèmes tonals de ces langues — qui distinguent, selon les cas, trois ou quatre registres — s'expliquent en effet comme la résultante d'un système « occidental commun » de trois registres, lequel constituait lui-même une innovation par rapport au système originel (« sara-bongo-baguirmien commun ») de deux registres [...] La branche « occidentale » s'est à son tour subdivisée en au moins trois rameaux18 : yulu, fer (ou kara de Birao) et « sara » (ce dernier rameau, provisoirement illustré par le mbay de Moïssala, le ngambay, le kenga, le kaba-na et le bagiro, [...] [p. 95:] Les caractéristiques tonales — communes au bagiro, au mbay, au ngambay, au kenga et au kaba-na — sur lesquelles on fonde la spécificité des langues sara sont les suivantes20 : [...] la préservation du scheme * BM est d'ailleurs irrégulière en mbay et en kenga (BM ou BB)
tone_statements.translation: An ongoing comparative study of the tone systems of several of them tends to prove that a 'western' branch, made up of the languages spoken in CAR and Chad (map III), split off historically from the original whole: the tone systems of these languages — which distinguish, as the case may be, three or four registers — are explained as the outcome of a 'common western' system of three registers, itself an innovation with respect to the original ('common Sara-Bongo-Bagirmi') system of two registers [...] The 'western' branch in turn subdivided into at least three sub-branches: Yulu, Fer (or Kara of Birao) and 'Sara' (this last sub-branch, provisionally illustrated by Mbay of Moïssala, Ngambay, Kenga, Kaba-na and Bagiro, [...] [p. 95:] The tonal characteristics — common to Bagiro, Mbay, Ngambay, Kenga and Kaba-na — on which the specificity of the Sara languages is founded are the following: [...] the preservation of the *LM scheme is moreover irregular in Mbay and in Kenga (LM or LL)
tone_statements.locator: pp. 93 (branch + register statement), 95-96 (section 'Les caractéristiques tonales', Kenga columns), fn. 20 p. 95 (sources: kenga = Vandame 1968)
tone_statements.summary: Kenga treated as a three-register (Low/Mid/High level-tone) western SBB language of the 'sara' branch; nominal schemes BB, BM, HB and tone-defined verb classes exemplified with Kenga forms from Vandame 1968; the three-register system is a shared western-SBB innovation over proto-SBB two registers.

sources.citation: Vandame, Charles. 1975. Notes sur l'organisation sociale, l'histoire, la vie rituelle, à Sara, village Kenga (Hadjeraï du Tchad). Journal de la Société des Africanistes 45(1): 69-114. DOI 10.3406/jafr.1975.1764.
sources.note: Ethnography read on Persée (PDF download could not be reached by automated download). Only linguistic remark is fn. 1 p. 69: 'les mots kenga ont été transcrits sans noter les tons ni les longueurs vocaliques'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2020. Central Sudanic Languages. Author manuscript (chapter for an OUP handbook of African languages), 13 pp. HAL halshs-03097024.
sources.note: Family-level overview: 'tone systems that may include up to four contrastive levels'; a typological table lists Kenga (possessive suffixes, SVO, noun-genitive). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Jacob, Peggy. 2017. Information structure in Sara-Bagirmi: A comparative approach to the synchronic state and diachronic development in the expression of information structure, with special attention to predicate-centered focus types. PhD dissertation, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, 197 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on word stress in Kenga (the words 'stress'/'accent' occur only for German/English examples). p. 22: the six languages studied, Kenga included, are 'tone languages with three level tones' (H/M/L), and fn. 6 notes that the Kenga literature marks all three tones; Kenga data drawn from Neukom 2010, Palayer 2004, Vandame 1968.

sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2009. Entre lac Albert et lac Tchad : l'expansion sara-bongo-baguirmienne. In Migrations et mobilité dans le bassin du Tchad (Maroua colloquium), 13 pp. HAL halshs-00348136.
sources.note: Comparative/historical; defines tones as pitch contrasts in SBB and gives Kenga cognates. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal & Pierre Nougayrol. 2008. Les langues soudaniques centrales : essai d'évaluation. Sprache und Geschichte in Afrika (SUGIA), 17 pp. HAL halshs-00348133.
sources.note: SBB languages have two-, three- or four-level tone systems; *SBB had two tones, western languages (Kenga among them, under *OCC > *SARA) added a third; Kenga appears in comparative lexical rows. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2006. Présentation des langues Sara-Bongo-Baguirmiennes. In P. Boyeldieu, P. Nougayrol & P. Palayer, Lexique comparatif historique des langues Sara-Bongo-Baguirmiennes (document électronique), 24 pp. Paris: CNRS-LLACAN.
sources.note: Comparative phonology of the SBB group (consonant, vowel and tone correspondence formulae). Kenga (source: Palayer 2004, Vandame 1968) is a 'western'/*OCC language with a three-register tone system; p. 9 notes Kenga has developed a vowel-length opposition in the initial syllable (CVCV/CV:CV). No mention of stress or accent.

Not a statement of the tone inventory.
